title: Deprecation without an Executable Retirement Plan
pattern: An API or service is marked deprecated (compiler annotations, warning logs) while callers can continue or add usage indefinitely, because migration and retirement are advisory only: no resources, tooling, enforcement policy, or decommissioning deadline backs the deprecation.
why_bad: Migration is repeatedly deferred as teams prioritize features, warnings lose force and become "alert fatigue", and both the obsolete and successor implementations must be maintained indefinitely in "dual-system purgatory", doubling operational cost and dragging down system evolution [292, 721, 723, 728].
detection: Long-standing deprecated entry points (e.g. `#[deprecated]` older than a major version, or a superseded service) that lack (a) an enforced no-new-use policy such as build-time or commit-time blocks on new invocations, (b) a staffed migration path for existing callers, or (c) documentation specifying a concrete turndown/decommissioning date. Warnings alone do not establish a cutover [297, 727].
counterexample: Valid for public open-source libraries with stable ABI guarantees (e.g., standard libraries) where code must be preserved forever, and for public-facing SDKs where backward compatibility is promised indefinitely to retain user goodwill [738]. Mark as `Context-dependent`.
fix: Move deprecation to a compulsory model: assign migration ownership and resources, publish the replacement and a strict retirement date, add backsliding linters that reject new usages, and actively run automated migrations of existing callers [297, 724, 725, 733, 734]. For services with unknown consumers, use controlled dependency-discovery exercises (e.g. temporary planned outages) only where the service contract and safety requirements permit them; retire once dependencies are handled.
source: Software Engineering at Google, Chapter 15, "Types of Deprecation - Advisory Deprecation" [292, 297, 721, 723, 727, 728]
